_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- West Virginia holiday calendars, 2026-2031. Loaded
through add_holidays alongside sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_westvirginia.json.
SOURCE OF THE DATES: W. Va. Code 2-2-1(a), read verbatim from the West Virginia
Legislature's own code site on 2026-08-25. SOURCE OF WHICH DAYS COUNT: W. Va.
R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6), read verbatim from the Supreme Court of Appeals' published
Rules of Civil Procedure. Those are two different lists and they are not the
same list -- see below. This calendar encodes the CIVIL one.
== WEST VIRGINIA HAS TWO OFFICIAL HOLIDAY LISTS AND THEY DISAGREE ==========
R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6) and R. App. P. 39(a) each define "legal holiday" for their
own body of rules, and the definitions are not identical. The engine keys a
holiday calendar by JURISDICTION AND YEAR only, so one `wv` calendar has to
serve both, and it cannot serve both correctly.
THE IRREDUCIBLE DIFFERENCE IS JUNETEENTH. R. App. P. 39(a) names "Juneteenth
Day" expressly. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6) does not, and cannot reach it indirectly:
6(a)(6)(C) covers a day "declared a holiday by the Governor or President of the
United States or any other legal holiday so designated by the West Virginia
Legislature" -- it omits CONGRESS, which is what created Juneteenth National
Independence Day, and W. Va. Code 2-2-1(a) does not list Juneteenth either.
THIS CALENDAR OMITS JUNETEENTH, AND THAT IS THE SAFE DIRECTION, NOT A
PREFERENCE. Including it would roll CIVIL deadlines off 19 June that the civil
rule does not roll -- a LATER date, which is the direction that misses a
filing. Omitting it makes APPELLATE deadlines landing on 19 June compute one
day EARLY, which files early. This file follows the rule already stated for the
Pennsylvania calendars in api/_lib/deadline-engine.js: an honestly incomplete
calendar is safer than one padded with days a rule does not make holidays.
The consequence is real and is disclosed on every appellate row in the seed.
Note the divergence does NOT bite in 2026: 20 June 2026 is a Saturday, so West
Virginia Day is observed Friday 19 June 2026 and that date is in this calendar
anyway. The first year it can bite is a year where 19 June is a business day
and is not already West Virginia Day observed.
== "LINCOLN'S DAY" IS THE DAY AFTER THANKSGIVING, NOT 12 FEBRUARY ==========
READ THIS BEFORE 'CORRECTING' ANY ENTRY BELOW. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6)(A) names
"Lincoln's Birthday", which reads like Indiana's 12 February holiday. It is
not. The rule counts "the day set aside BY STATUTE for observing" it, and the
only day the statute sets aside under Lincoln's name is 2-2-1(a)(11): "The day
after Thanksgiving Day is 'Lincoln's Day'." R. App. P. 39(a) uses the statutory
name "Lincoln's Day" and confirms the reading. No West Virginia statute read on
2026-08-25 sets aside 12 February, and no February entry appears below.
2-2-1(b), verbatim: "If a holiday otherwise described in subsection (a) of this
section falls on a Sunday, then the following Monday is the legal holiday. If a
holiday otherwise described in subsection (a) of this section falls on a
Saturday, then the preceding Friday is the legal holiday: Provided, That this
subsection shall not apply to subdivisions (13), (14), and (15), subsection (a)
of this section." So election days, Susan B. Anthony Day and gubernatorial days
never shift; the twelve named holidays do, in BOTH directions. Only the
fixed-date ones can shift at all: 1 January, 20 June, 4 July, 11 November and
25 December.
THE BACKWARD SHIFT PUTS A HOLIDAY IN THE PREVIOUS YEAR. When 1 January falls
on a Saturday the legal holiday is the preceding Friday, 31 December -- a date
belonging to the earlier year's calendar. 2027-12-31 is filed under 2027 here
for that reason, and deliberately NOT also under 2028: the engine resolves a
holiday by the year of the date and the endpoint rejects a date whose year does
not match its calendar, so a 2028-filed entry would be silently unreachable.
The generator's own self-check caught it filed under both.
== ELECTION DAYS: STATEWIDE ONLY, AND THE REST ARE NOT ENUMERABLE ==========
2-2-1(a)(13) makes any general, primary or special election day a holiday
"throughout the state, a political subdivision of the state, a district or an
incorporated city, town or village in which the election is conducted", and
R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6)(B) reaches an election held "in the State, or in the county
in which the circuit court sits". Only the two STATEWIDE elections are
enumerable and only those appear below: the primary, "the second Tuesday in
May" of each even year (W. Va. Code 3-5-1), and the general, "the Tuesday next
after the first Monday in November of each even year" (W. Va. Code 3-1-31(a)).
MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS ADD NO DATES, which is narrower than the same problem in
Indiana and is worth knowing: 3-1-31(a) requires that "all local municipal
elections shall be held concurrently with a regularly scheduled statewide
primary or general election". COUNTY SPECIAL ELECTIONS STILL DO. A special
election in the county where the circuit court sits is a legal holiday for that
court under 6(a)(6)(B) and cannot be enumerated in advance. A deadline computed
across one will be EARLY, not late.
== ALSO NOT ENUMERABLE, AND ALSO EARLY-FAILING ============================
2-2-1(a)(15) gubernatorial days of special observance, and 2-2-1(c) statewide
employee days off, which "may, for all courts, be treated as if it were a legal
holiday". Both are declared ad hoc. Neither is below.
Susan B. Anthony Day (2-2-1(a)(14)) needs no separate entry: it IS general
election day in even years.
No 2025 calendar is provided even though the restyled civil rules took effect
2025-01-01. A 2025 trigger therefore draws a NOT_PROVISIONED refusal rather
than a date computed against a missing calendar.

authority.citation: W. Va. Code 2-2-1(a) (legal holidays), as applied to civil time computation by W. Va. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6)
authority.note: Generated 2026-08-25 from W. Va. Code 2-2-1(a) (the dates) and W. Va. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6) (which days count for civil computation), both read verbatim. Twelve named holidays plus statewide election days in even years. EXCLUDES JUNETEENTH -- neither 2-2-1(a) nor R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6) lists it, and 6(a)(6)(C) omits Congress from the bodies whose declarations count, so the federal designation does not reach the civil rule. R. App. P. 39(a) DOES name it, and this one calendar cannot serve both lists; see the file readme. "Lincoln's Day" is the day after Thanksgiving per 2-2-1(a)(11), NOT 12 February. Weekend shift is both-way per 2-2-1(b) (Sunday -> following Monday, Saturday -> preceding Friday) and does not apply to election days or gubernatorial days. Gubernatorial days of special observance (2-2-1(a)(15)), statewide employee days off (2-2-1(c)) and county special elections (R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6)(B)) are declared ad hoc and are not enumerable; a deadline computed across one is EARLY, never late.
